text: Those associations include not just the Webster's meaning but the slang meaning — and, for many who grew up in church, the taught “seminary meaning.”

The serpent's first recorded words are an attack not on the text but on its meaning — __“Yea, hath God said?”__ (Genesis 3:1) — and that has been the strategy ever since: what cannot be deleted can be re-glossed.

Scripture's symbols are built the same way: the meaning of a symbol is not stored in its label but established by every place the word is used and every word it stands beside, line upon line, across the whole of the text.
Bread is the word: __“man doth not live by bread only, but by *every word* that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

Disciples do forsake all — Peter says so five verses later and is not corrected (Matthew 19:27), and __“whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple”__ (Luke 14:33) — but mark what no disciple ever did: buy the field.

The next day the same crowd hunts Him down, and He tells them what they missed: __“Ye seek me, not because ye saw the sym:sym-sign[signs], but because ye did *eat of the loaves*, and were filled”__ (John 6:26) — they had eaten the sign without reading it.

That is what this book set out to make of its reader: not a keeper of our conclusions but a scribe instructed — one who can take a text he has never been taught, derive it from what Scripture itself defined, mark honestly what remains under test, and go gather the uses.
That is a similitude: not a story about the truth, but the truth rehearsed.
She did not merely survive; she entered the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5).

Clement of Rome, writing while men who knew the apostles still lived, says the spies gave her __“a sign… a scarlet thread, thereby showing beforehand that through the blood of the Lord there shall be redemption unto all them that believe,”__ and draws the conclusion for us: __“not only faith, but prophecy, is found in the woman”__ (1 Clement 12).
On Passover night He fulfilled the casting too — not as the stiller of the storm but as the man given to it:
So the sign of Jonah is not only the Passion; it is the gospel going out to the nations after the resurrection.

Not __“accept this fact,”__ but __“repent ye, and believe”__ — turn, trust, and obey; for to sym:sym-belief[believe], as the link:/books/symbolic-language/knowing-faith-love-and-belief/[Love, Knowing, Faith, and Belief] chapter will prove, is to obey.
The gospel is the message Jesus _taught_, not merely the message _about_ Jesus.
The fault lay not with the covenant but with the people — __“my covenant they brake.”__
Jesus did not come to abolish the law, nor to complete it and retire it, but to fill it full — to preach it in its fullness, packing back the weight the surface reading had drained away.
_This_ is the message Jesus taught — not a new religion about Himself, but the ancient covenant of the kingdom, renewed and written on the heart.
That is what sym:sym-belief[believe] means in Scripture’s mouth: not thinking a thing true, but trusting enough to obey.

Read it as Scripture defines it, and the turning of the nations that closed the last chapter stands revealed for what it is: not the spread of information about a man, but the kingdom of God going forth to fill the earth.
He kept the law — perfectly: __“Which of you convinceth me of sin?”__ (John 8:46); not to destroy but to fulfil (Matthew 5:17).

__“Love *does not envy*”__ — the tenth commandment kept; __“does not seek its own… thinks no *evil*”__ — no ill worked to a neighbor; __“does not rejoice in *lawlessness*, but rejoices in the sym:sym-truth[truth]”__ — and __“thy *law* is the truth”__ (Psalm 119:142).

Scripture keeps the pattern consistently: hope's object is unseen by definition — __“hope that is *seen* is not hope… but if we hope for that we see not, then do we with *patience* wait for it”__ (Romans 8:24-25) — and the patience is faithfulness holding while the thing stays out of sight.

But He has named _three_ things, not one, each a word Scripture has already filled with meaning; and the small word fastened to each is _the_ — not _a_ way, _a_ truth, _a_ life, but _the_, the particular one God defines.
So a person’s __“way”__ is not where they are headed but _how they go_ — their conduct, their manner of life.
Which is why the first followers of Jesus were not called Christians but were known, simply, as __“the Way”__ — and when Paul was charged with belonging to it, here is how he owned the name:
Not __“thy law is true,”__ but __“thy law _is_ the truth”__ — the standard itself, the measure by which everything else is weighed.

The life _was_ the light — and light is a defined symbol with link:/books/symbolic-language/light-and-darkness/[its own chapter ahead]: not truth in the abstract, but the law lived where men can see it (Matthew 5:16).footnote:fn07light516[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/light-and-darkness/[Light and Darkness] chapter.]
The life does not merely exist; it shows.

It must be _prepared_: __“make straight in the desert a highway for our God”__ (Isaiah 40:3) — not a work of shovels but of repentance, the cry John the Baptist took up, clearing the obstacles off the covenant road.
Set the three side by side and they are not separate claims but one reality seen from three angles.
It does not mean to _bar_ the way but to _preserve_ it.
Not a new road to God, but the original road, walked perfectly and thrown open.
To ask __“in my name”__ is not to invoke a syllable but to ask _as one who belongs to Him_ — within His will, on His terms, inside the relationship.
David offered to build God a house of stone; God replies, __“the LORD telleth thee that *he will make thee an house*”__ (2 Samuel 7:11) — not cedar but sons: the house _of David_.
To __“sym:sym-belief[believe] on his name”__ (John 1:12) is not to credit a title but to enter that covenant in trusting obedience.
The mouth full of the name, the ear turned from the covenant that fills it: such prayer does not merely go unanswered, it offends.
The last petition asks the covenant God for the covenant deliverance: __“lead us not into temptation, but *deliver us* from evil”__ (Matthew 6:13).

Trial itself is not prayed away — the manna was given to prove — the plea is to be brought _through_ the proving and out of the destroyer’s hand, with the promise standing behind it: God __“will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a *way to escape*”__ (1 Corinthians 10:13).
The symbols do not merely repeat; they compound.

God's servants do not merely carry His mark; He wears them: __“though Coniah… were the *signet upon my right hand*, yet would I pluck thee thence”__ (Jeremiah 22:24) — and to faithful Zerubbabel, __“I… will make thee as a *signet*: for I have *chosen* thee”__ (Haggai 2:23).
The law prices persons in silver — not as a figure of speech, but as statute: a man vowed to God is redeemed __“by thy estimation”__, in sanctuary shekels (Leviticus 27:2-8).

The money is called __“a *memorial*”__ (Exodus 30:16) — the same word the law uses for the sign bound between the eyes (on the forehead) — and it is not banked but appointed __“for the service of the tabernacle.”__

__“Put away… according to the law”__ — divorce, not as concession but as obedience, demanded by the men who trembled at the commandment; and Nehemiah enforces the same, holding up Solomon as the proof of where the strange wives lead: __“even him did outlandish women cause to sin”__ (Nehemiah 13:26).
To the married he gives the absolute rule and names its source: __“I command, yet *not I, but the Lord*, Let not the wife depart from her husband”__ (1 Corinthians 7:10).

The case is heard __“according to *law*”__ (Esther 1:15), and the concern of the court is not jealousy but obedience across the whole realm: __“this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto *all women*, so that they shall *despise their husbands*”__ (Esther 1:17).

One formula, one lesson: the King’s wife must obey, or the estate passes — not because the King is petty, but because the whole land learns from the queen; the covenant marriage is public, and its breach teaches rebellion to every house in the empire.
The wife earned the stoning; the Husband takes the stroke; and rising, He is free to wed her again — not under the old contract she shattered, but new.

That is why Hosea, God’s sign-and-similitude marriage, must not only endure his wife’s adultery but _buy her back_ — __“So I *bought her* to me for fifteen pieces of silver”__ (Hosea 3:2) — and why the reunion is a fresh betrothal in the vocabulary this book keeps finding at the center: __“I will *betroth thee* unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], and in sym:sym-judgment[judgment]… and thou shalt sym:sym-knowing[know] the LORD”__ (Hosea 2:19-20).
The Gospels are precise about what she touched — not the cloak, but its __“border”__ (Luke 8:44), its __“hem”__ (Matthew 9:20).
So the fringe on the wing is not an aid to reflection; it is a trigger for obedience — __“not a forgetful hearer, but a *doer* of the work”__ (James 1:25).
Even the burning ones wear the covering: the seraphim, six-winged, use four of their wings not to fly but to cover themselves before the fire (Isaiah 6:2).
The widow and the fatherless are not only the poor down the street; they are the covenant people themselves, severed from the God who was their Husband and their Father.

Scripture makes bread the word of God — __“man doth not live by sym:sym-bread[bread] only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3) — and the sym:sym-garment[garment], as the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] chapter showed, is the righteous deeds of the saints — deeds He ordains and grants her to do (Ephesians 2:10; Revelation 19:8).
The gleaning law itself encodes the ratio — not in a number, but in a shape.
The law does not merely say a remnant will be left; the ratio is built into the field.

The prophetic picture of the kingdom is __“they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree”__ (Micah 4:4) — and that is not a poet's flourish but a quotation, for the phrase first describes a real population at a real date: __“Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree… all the days of Solomon”__ (1 Kings 4:25).
The gleaning law does not only fix how many survive the harvest.

Isaiah states the same structure as government: __“The heaven is my *throne*, and the earth is my *footstool*”__ (Isaiah 66:1) — throne and footstool are not scenery but offices, the seat of rule and the territory under it.

When Jesus warns of __“hell fire,”__ this is His word — and He keeps it strictly apart from hades: the gates of *hades* shall not prevail (Matthew 16:18), but it is in *Gehenna* that God is __“able to *destroy* both soul and body”__ (Matthew 10:28).

There is no chamber constructed for the wicked in some corner of creation; there is the unshielded presence of the Holy One, and the question Scripture presses is not *where you are sent* but *what you are wearing when you meet Him*.
Permanent, final, past atonement; not endless dying, but a death that holds.

The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16) is the fourth parable in a chain of parables, told in the furniture of the day, and its own spoken point is not the architecture of the afterlife but the sufficiency of the Scriptures: __“They have *Moses and the prophets*; let them hear them… If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead”__ (Luke 16:29, 31).
The gnashing is the wicked man's answer to *that* — and its end is not an endless scream but a dissolution: __“the desire of the wicked shall perish.”__
__“The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy *shade* upon thy right hand”__ (Psalm 121:5) — the LORD does not merely cast a shadow; He _is_ the shade.
Justice is righteousness under a second English name — not an abstraction to be argued about but the commandments done, toward God and toward one’s neighbor.
The man who renders the weak their due is not merely imitating God’s character; he is inside it.

And Jesus set the two figures side by side in the same breath as His teaching on freedom: __“the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the *Son abideth ever*”__ (John 8:35) — the Son is the one who stays in the Father’s house by nature, and the freed slave who loves his Master stays by choice.
Not “there is no God” as a theory, but as a way of living — as though no one were watching and nothing were owed.
And the Lord Himself draws the line — not between those who hear and those who don’t, but between two men who hear the very same words:

Wisdom, then, is not cleverness but obedience: __“a good sym:sym-understanding[understanding] have all they that do his commandments”__ (Psalm 111:10); __“keep therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom”__ (Deuteronomy 4:6).
What divides them is not their purity as a literal virgin in the modern sense, but their store:

On the olive-nation's own hill stood the press, and there the Lord was crushed under the weight of death — His sweat __“as it were great drops of blood”__ (Luke 22:44) — and gave up the oil of a perfect obedience: __“not my will, but thine, be done”__ (Luke 22:42).
Between the fool and the wise there is finally one question — the question this whole book keeps asking: not what you heard, but whether you did it.
Which tells you at once what darkness is — not ignorance, but concealment.
God does not weigh worship by its sincerity but by whose commandments shape it.
=== Not Terror, but Obedience
We are not saved by our works, but we can be condemned by willful, unrepentant breaking of his commands and denying their truth.

Jesus did not come to destroy the Law or the Prophets but to *fulfill* them — link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[to fill them full], to bring them to fullness (Matthew 5:17).footnote:fn32fulfil[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter.]
Now mark what kind of case that is: not a point at all, but a letter — a letter the promise itself guards.
From the first page of Scripture the lights of heaven are given a job, and it is not merely to glow.
Mark where the verse sets the perfection: not on the Father alone, but on what stands *with* Him — the Greek is _par’ hō_, *beside whom*.
The sign is _nes_ — not a mere signal but a *standard*, raised high for every eye, the ensign-word of the __“root of Jesse”__ (Isaiah 11:10).

The word under __“throne”__ is _kisse’_ — and the last chapter opened this door: the Hebrew word for the *full moon*, _keseh_, is spelled with the very same consonants; not a resemblance, but letter-identity in the text itself.
__“Sides”__ is _yarketh_ — not a side but the *farthest recess* of a thing: the innermost hold of Jonah's ship (Jonah 1:5), the deepest __“sides of the cave”__ where David hid (1 Samuel 24:3).
It is *one*: the merchant found __“one pearl of great price”__ and stopped collecting, for the kingdom is not a collection but one bride, bought whole.
The Exodus is not only history; it is the similitude of the Fall of Babylon — scene for scene, as Jonah was scene for scene the Passion.
The priesthood gone serpentine does not merely join the dragons of the nations; it *swallows* them — it out-devours the devourers and rides what remains.

The dragon fells a third of heaven's host not with claws but with its tail — by the prophet that teaches lies — for __“the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are *destroyed*”__ (Isaiah 9:16).
Messiah does not merely suffer the verb; He performs it: Messiah shall *cut a covenant*.

When the vineyard is judged, God grounds the clouds first: __“I will also *command the clouds* that they *rain no rain* upon it”__ (Isaiah 5:6) — and Amos names the resulting drought exactly: __“not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but *of hearing the words of the LORD*”__ (Amos 8:11).
Three times in one chapter, the mourners themselves keep saying the word — because the thing that stuns them most is not that Babylon fell, but how fast.
The shortness of the word is not only a threat, and Scripture will not let the reader forget it.

The vision that seems slow is not therefore false: __“the vision is yet for an *appointed time*, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, *wait for it*; because it will *surely come*, it will not tarry”__ (Habakkuk 2:3).

The contrast is the whole point: AI does not interpret Scripture for us, and it must not be trusted to — but the meaning is already there, recoverable by anyone, or anything, willing to follow the method rather than lean on inherited opinion.
What forces the right answer is not the cleverness of the reader but the discipline of the process.
The flood is not only the enemy’s weapon; it is also how the enemy ends.
The first two readings are not false, but they stop short.
In the new creation there is no more sea — and so no more islands: not because the set-apart vanish, but because nothing remains to be set apart from.
Mountain and sea are not two unrelated pictures but two halves of one map: the governing and the governed, the rule and the ruled.
And these come up not from the garden but __“from the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Daniel 7:3) — the same peoples, seen now as predators rising from the restless deep.

We have already seen that the law was not abolished but filled full, and that the covenant-name is everlasting — and the food law is part of that law; here it stands as the very ground of the verdict.
Grass is not only the picture of frailty; it is also the field God farms.
So when Jesus says the same, He is not inventing an image but citing one:
The *tares* are not the wheat's own husk but a weed sown among it — darnel, which *mimics* the wheat so closely that the two cannot be told apart until the ear forms.

Grain ground and baked becomes bread, and __“man doth not live by sym:sym-bread[bread] only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3) — the bread is the word.
He was not merely at a loss for words; he was muzzled — silenced the way a power greater than his own silences what it overrules, with no defense in his mouth because he had none on his back.
The rag is blood-stained — fouled by the very iniquities the verse goes on to name — not because doing right is wrong, but because the doer is unclean.
Jesus therefore stooped to wash them: not a second baptism, but the daily cleansing of the walk that keeps the garment clean.
To be without the garment is to be naked, and nakedness, from the garden onward, is not nudity but exposure — the covenant covering gone, the shame seen.

The armor is God's own war-dress, put on because no man could — which is what __“the whole armour *of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:11) says when it is allowed to mean it: not armor from His stores, but the armor He wears, lent to the soldier.
And how a covenant binds not one wearer but a whole people together is the next symbol: the bow.
The very first bow-covenant, then, is struck not with one tribe but with _every nation on earth_ — a universal covenant of sym:sym-peace[peace], set over all the families of the ground.
He conquers not by the shot but by the bow itself — he wins the nations by _covenant_.
So it was with the first kingdom built against heaven: it was founded not on a weapon but on a name.

Not _make us_ a name but _I will make thy_ name — a covenant given, not grasped; and where Babel’s name was built to keep one people from scattering, Abraham’s name is given to bless _all the families of the earth_.
The second name is what God does with such a heart. _Israel_ — to _prevail_ with _God_ — is given not for bloodline but for what happened in the dark: he held on, __“and prevailed.”__

The Jew is __“one inwardly”__ (Romans 2:28-29) — and Paul's definition carries Judah's name inside it: Judah means *praise* — __“Now will I *praise* the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah”__ (Genesis 29:35) — and the verse lands exactly there: the Jew inwardly is he __“whose *praise* is not of men, but of God.”__
Peter says it of the gathered church: __“which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”__ (1 Peter 2:10).

Revelation seals the reading: the two witnesses __“are the *two olive trees*, and the *two candlesticks*”__ (Revelation 11:4) — and a candlestick, by the book's own key, is an assembly (Revelation 1:20): not two men, but two covenant peoples bearing witness.
Moses' _because_ is the definition: the visible sign is not merely insufficient — worn without the substance, it is the ground of the indictment.

Paul writes the beast's definition into covenant standing itself: __“he is not a Jew, which is one *outwardly*… But he is a Jew, which is one *inwardly*; and circumcision is that of the heart”__ (Romans 2:28-29).
The Old Testament's last swine verses aim inward — not at Rome, but at covenant men wearing the beast's structure.

God says of the prophets, __“I have multiplied visions, and used *similitudes*, by the ministry of the prophets”__ (Hosea 12:10) — and the Signs & Similitudes chapter showed what that ministry cost: Hosea's marriage was the similitude, Ezekiel's siege-brick was the similitude; the prophets did not merely speak the pictures, they *lived* them, by obedience.
The theater is not the reason the command binds — it binds because God spoke it — but it is the reason revealed: obedience is a role in the play, and the prophets teach us to want the part.

[[sym-fornication]]Fornication, whoredom:: Spiritual unfaithfulness — breaking covenant with God to go after other gods and kingdoms; not merely the physical sin. The out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom. +

[[sym-jew]]Jew:: In covenant contexts, one in the covenant — “he is a Jew, which is one *inwardly*,” while some “say they are Jews, and are not.” The name is Judah's, and Judah means praise — “Now will I praise the LORD” — so Paul's definition lands on the name itself: the Jew inwardly is he “whose praise is not of men, but of God.” The word also walks in plain dress, ethnic and religious; context decides which coat it wears. +

[[sym-week]]Week:: A seven — _shavua_, a unit of sevens, and not only of days: Laban decodes it in the text — “Fulfil her *week*… yet seven other *years*” — and Jacob serves seven years for the week named; the jubilee is counted as “seven sabbaths of years,” and Daniel’s seventy weeks are sevens of years — unpointed, seventy sevens that open into seventy jubilees. The Feast of Weeks runs the same count in days — seven sevens to the fiftieth — the jubilee modeled a day for a sym:sym-year[year]. +
Then came the realization that we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against powers in high places — and no protocol reforms those.
